John Philpot
jŏn fĭl´pŏt
n. (John Philpot, c. 1516–1555, Archdeacon of Winchester, examined fourteen times under Mary and burned at Smithfield on 18 December 1555)
English Philpot, a diminutive of Philip; also written Philpott.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John Philpot was a gentleman's son of Hampshire, a good Hebraist, and Archdeacon of Winchester under Edward. In the Convocation of 1553 he spoke against the restoration of the mass to its face and was imprisoned for it, and he spent eighteen months being examined — fourteen separate hearings before Bonner, Gardiner and others — of which he wrote his own detailed accounts and smuggled them out. They are among the most valuable documents of the English Reformation, because they show the arguments actually used on both sides rather than the martyrologist's summary. He was learned, quick and sometimes sharp to the point of rudeness with his examiners. Burned at Smithfield in December 1555, he is said to have kissed the stake and called it his school. Luk 21:15 is the promise he relied on: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.” Act 6:10 records it fulfilled in Stephen, and Psa 119:46 states the duty: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an examination as a careful search or inquiry; an interrogation; and to gainsay as to contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true.

expand to see more

EXAMINA'TION, n. The act of examining; a careful search or inquiry, with a view to discover truth.

3. In judicial proceedings, a careful inquiry into facts by testimony.

GAINSAY', v.t. To contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true.

Key Scripture

Luk 21:15 — "For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist."

Act 6:10 — "And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake."

Mat 10:18 — "And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles."

Psa 119:46 — "I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed."

Modern Corruption

Philpot wrote down what his examiners actually said, and that is why his Examinations are worth more than a hundred pages of praise for him.

expand to see more

Martyrologies tend to give the martyr's courage and omit the argument, which quietly suggests that the issue was temperament rather than truth. Philpot's records do the opposite: they set out the Roman case on the sacrament, the church and tradition in his opponents' own words, with his replies, so a reader can judge. Mat 10:18 says believers will be “brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them,” and a testimony is content, not merely bearing. The documents are a service to the church precisely because they are not hagiography.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that Luk 21:15 promises wisdom rather than exemption. The verse is sometimes read as a guarantee of deliverance, and Philpot's case shows what it actually gives: his adversaries could not gainsay nor resist him, and they burned him anyway. The promise is that the witness will be adequate, not that it will be accepted, and the Christian under examination may therefore prepare his answer and leave the outcome where Psa 119:46 leaves it, speaking before kings and not being ashamed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek stoma (G4750), a mouth; antilego (G483), to gainsay; anthistemi (G436), to resist.

expand to see more

Greek stoma (G4750) — a mouth, hence utterance; Luke 21:15.

Greek antepo and antilego (G483) — to speak against, to gainsay; Luke 21:15.

Greek anthistemi (G436) — to set against, to resist; Luke 21:15, Acts 6:10.

Greek marturion (G3142) — a testimony; Matthew 10:18.

Hebrew eduth (H5715) — testimonies; Psalm 119:46.

Usage

"“I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist” (Luk 21:15) — wisdom promised, not exemption."

"“they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake” (Act 6:10) — fulfilled in Stephen, who also died."

"“I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46) — the duty stated."
